title: Monitor agent flows and their cost

sentences.text: Thursday at Contoso.
Employees complain that some of their tickets were never created.
The I T agent calls a flow named Create ticket, and somewhere it fails.
On the same day, finance asks a second question: how much are these agent flows costing us?
Two questions, one place to look.
By the end of this class you will know where to find the failed runs, how to fix them, and how the bill is counted.
Here is the picture to keep.
A flow in production needs a dashboard, like a car.
The dashboard tells you whether everything is running fine, and how much fuel you use.
In Copilot Studio that dashboard has three tabs, and the fuel is measured in Copilot Credits, the unit for Copilot Studio capacity.
Health on one side, fuel on the other.
The three tabs each have one job.
Overview shows the flow details: name, description, connections and owners, plus the most recent runs.
From Overview you can also turn the flow off or delete it.
Activity shows the run history, with the status and duration of each run.
Analytics summarizes the activity: the number of runs, the error rate, and the trends over time.
Activity is where you work.
Select a run to open its details and see exactly where it failed.
You can also select several runs at once to resubmit them, which means sending them again, or to cancel the ones still in progress.
One more detail for the exam: Analytics can take up to thirty minutes to reflect new runs, so a missing number there is not always a problem.
Your turn.
The team wants to see each failed run of Create ticket, open its details, and send the failed runs again after the fix.
Which tab do they open?
Activity, because it keeps all run details?
Overview, because it lists the latest runs?
Or Analytics, because it charts the error rate?
Decide before I answer.
Activity.
It holds the full run history, the details of each run, and Resubmit.
Analytics only gives the numbers, and Overview only the latest runs.
Watch Contoso do it.
They open the Activity tab of Create ticket.
Two runs have the status failed.
They open the details, and both stopped at the same step: the Dataverse connection.
They fix the connection, select the two failed runs, and resubmit them.
The tickets are created.
Then they open Analytics to watch the error rate come down over the next half hour.
Now the fuel.
Each action in an agent flow consumes capacity: thirteen Copilot Credits for every hundred actions.
Tests in the designer or in the test chat, called test runs, do not consume capacity.
And users with a Microsoft three six five Copilot license are not charged when the flow is triggered with the trigger called when an agent calls the flow.
Let us do the math the exam likes.
Contoso's flow has twenty actions, and it runs five hundred times.
Twenty times five hundred is ten thousand actions.
Ten thousand divided by a hundred is a hundred blocks, and each block costs thirteen credits.
So about one thousand three hundred Copilot Credits.
The tests they ran earlier in the designer added nothing to that number.
What happens when prepaid capacity runs out?
New runs are blocked.
The runs already in progress finish normally.
And the agent keeps responding in interactions that do not use flows.
The agent does not stop working completely, that is the trap.
To avoid interruptions, you can link a pay as you go plan, so the flows keep running when the prepaid capacity is gone.
Your turn.
In the middle of the day, Contoso's prepaid capacity runs out.
What happens?
The agent stops answering until capacity is added?
All runs in progress are cancelled right away?
Or new flow runs are blocked, the agent talks on?
Decide before I answer.
The third one.
Only new flow runs are blocked.
The agent keeps talking.
Copilot Credits are the single unit across all three harnesses, but what counts is different.
On the standard harness, credits are metered per event, at defined rates for each interaction type.

On the Microsoft Copilot harness, formerly the GitHub Copilot harness, billing is usage based: the language model tokens, the tools called, including knowledge and M C P, and the harness runtime itself.
The timing differs too.
Standard and Copilot chat agents accrue credits at runtime only, when a published agent handles interactions.
The Microsoft Copilot harness is the only one that bills from build time as well.
So authoring, previewing and evaluating also use credits.
And the Microsoft three six five Copilot license exception for authenticated users does not apply to the Microsoft Copilot harness.
Your turn.
Contoso's makers spent a week authoring and previewing a new agent.
Nothing was published yet, but Copilot Credits were consumed.
Which harness is the agent on?
The standard harness for agents?
The Microsoft Copilot harness?
Or the Copilot chat harness?
Decide before I answer.
The Microsoft Copilot harness.
It is the only one that bills from build time, so authoring, previewing and evaluating use credits.
The other two bill at runtime only.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness, four things drive consumption.
The model, because reasoning models meter premium tokens.
The organizational context the agent draws in.
The number of tools and actions.
And the complexity of the task and orchestration.
A Copilot Credits estimator helps you plan from representative scenarios, but treat its results as directional, a compass, not a quote.
Here are the steps.
In Copilot Studio, open the flows list and select your agent flow.
Review Overview: name, connections, owners and recent runs.
Go to Activity and review the status and duration of each run.
Select a failed run and open its details.
Select the failed runs and use Resubmit.
Open Analytics for the number of runs and the error rate.
Then estimate the cost at thirteen credits per hundred actions.
Back to Contoso.
The missing tickets were found in Activity, fixed at the connection, and resubmitted.
Finance got its number: about one thousand three hundred credits for five hundred runs.
Remember for the exam: Activity is history and resubmit, an empty tank blocks only new runs, test runs are free, and only the Microsoft Copilot harness bills from build time.
